author: Stocky
text:
This is my first attempt on a technical analysis of S&D. Also this is a first time I put into writing any kind of technical analysis regarding FX.

Homework Compression Part 1 LTF 15M

1. As PA moves between the supply and demand zones in this case there is a lot of compression

2. Buy orders get filled in on the retest of the demand zone and there is a effortless 40 pip rise do to previous CP

3. Not enough serious sell orders are found on the 4th retest of the supply zone and a bullish flag forms right below the supply line, the price breaks out of the flag and through the supply zone for another 50 pips.

4. As the price tests the former supply line, now a support it forms a bear flag and breaks effortlessly down 30 pips do to previous CP.

5. Again the price starts to wonder in between the supply and demand zones in mayor compression until it manages to enter the demand zone, pick up enough orders to reach the now many times tested and twice broken supply zone.

6. From here it is a fairly easy ride down with not much resistance found at the demand zone as it breaks it and heads straight down for 70 pips do to previous CP.

author: madwt
text:
This is my first post on this forum.

I like to digest an idea, mull it over for a while and then express the idea verbally to see if it makes sense. This is what I am doing here. Once I am comfortable I have digested the idea, the practice may begin. In this post, I am going to verbalise my understanding of compression, but more importantly, how it is of benefit to a trader.

Trading charts is similar to playing sport. In sport, we need to use different tactics at different places on the field. Have you watched Australia Ruby League (Australia football)? If so, what do you find in the middle of the field? You will find mud, blood, injuries and so on. It is not where you look to execute your key plays.

Rather, you want to execute your key plays where they count. This is near the try (score/goal/touch down) line. You do not use your key plays anywhere on the field. You wait until your team is in position, a place where you have an opportunity to score. Then, when the conditions are right, you execute your key plays. In trading, your key plays are your entry techniques and where you use them matters.

As a trader, we need to identify areas of opportunity, a place on the chart where the odds are significantly in our favour. Strong supply and demand levels provide this opportunity. These are places on a chart where a move may start from. This is where we can bring out our key plays out and score a touch-down.

At a strong supply level, we expect there to be an overwhelming volume of sell orders and price to fall. At a strong demand level, we expect there to be an overwhelming volume of buy orders and price to rise. However, like in our sports analogy, the team may be at the right place on the field, but your key players may not yet be positioned for the best possible opportunity. However, once everyone is in place, it’s time to go for the touch-down.

Once we are in the right position on a chart, how can we tell if the odds are significantly in our favour? That is the important question. In other words, if we are at a significant demand level and ready to short, what conditions would prevent price falling rapidly?

The only thing which will stop price falling (sessions times, news, etc. aside) are buy orders waiting to be consumed, pushing price back up, or stalling the fall. However, if there were no buy orders waiting to be consumed below the current price level, the selling pressure at a supply level would cause the price to fall rapidly. Price is free to drop until it once again reaches a demand level where new buyers are waiting.

This can be summarised as follows:

- We want to short at a strong supply level if we believe the buy orders lurking below the current price were consumed in the up move.

- We want to buy at a strong demand level if we believe thee sell orders lurking above the current price were consumed in the down move.

We know when we are at a supply or demand level. We can see this on the chart. The problem is, we cannot see how many buy orders are sitting below us, nor can we see how many sell orders are sitting above us. However, we can make an educated guess about what orders may be lurking by visually recognising what the consumption of previous orders looks like on a chart.

The visual recognition of the consumption of orders on a chart is called compression.

If price is moving up and compressing, the buy orders are being consumed. If the buy orders have been consumed, they are not lurking below the current price. As such, when price hits a strong supply level and selling pressure kicks in, price has a clear path to drop straight back through the area of compression. Price is free to drop as there are no pockets of buy orders waiting to be consumed. Price will drop until it reaches a demand level where new buyers are waiting.

Likewise, if price is moving down and compressing, the sell orders are being

consumed. If the sell orders have been consumed, they are not lurking above the current price. As such, when price hits a strong demand level and buying pressure kicks in, price has a clear path to climb straight up through the area of compression. Price climbs as there are no longer pockets of sell orders waiting to be consumed. Price is free to climb until it reaches a supply level where new sellers are waiting.

For this reason:

- An ideal reversal point for a short position is at a strong supply level where price compressed into the supply.

- An ideal reversal point for a long position is at a strong demand level where price compressed into the demand.

By knowing this, the demand and supply zones can define where you want to bring out your key plays, and the compression tells you it’s an ideal time to place your chips on the table. This is why recognising and understanding compression is important to price action trading.

In my next post, I will describe what compression looks like on a chart and what is happening inside the compression. I hope other people find this post useful.

author: madwt
text:
In my last post, I described what compression is and why it is important. However, I did not describe what compression looks like on screen. In this post, I will describe what compression looks like on screen so that compression may be more easily recognised.

Price will rise when there are more buy orders than sell orders. We can see this visually. Price is rising and making higher highs and higher lows. Therefore we know that the buyers are in charge and driving price higher. In the same way, price will fall when there are more sell orders than buy orders. We can see this visually. Price is falling and making lower lows and lower highs. Therefore, we know the sellers are in charge pushing price lower.

If prices are rising and the buyers are in charge that is good. We need the buyers to push prices up to a major supply level where we are patiently waiting to sell. However, when we are ready to sell, we want the buyers which have moved price up to our major supply level to be exhausted. We do not want to get into a fight with the buyers. If they are exhausted, the will put up a small fight, and then crumble under the selling pressure. In order words, we want their buys orders to have been all consumed. We do not want buyers to still be vigorously chasing price up.

What is important is the way price is moving on screen, not just the fact price is moving up or moving down. If price is moving up, buyers will be keen to join the up-trend, or add new longs to their existing bullish position. However, buyers will generally prefer to buy at a price which they perceive to be good value. In order to buy at a price of good value, buyers wait for a pull-back to get in at a better price. However, they dare not wait for too much of a pull-back or they may miss the boat. Buy orders will usually be placed and sit eagerly awaiting price to come back to the most recent minor demand level. This is the last place from which price moved up or the most recent minor swing low.

If this is the case, price dips into the most recent minor demand and the buy orders are consumed. The consumption of these orders shoots the price back up. How this looks on screen depends on the time frame, though will often appear as candles with long lower wicks. How far price moves up depends on the how many excited buyers there are. If there are a significant number of buyers, price will zoom! However, this is not the price action that forms compression. In compression, there will be enough buyers to push prices up, possibly creating long lower wicks, but once the buy orders at perceived good value are consumed, price will move up steadily again.

As the trend continues, the process repeats over. Price dips, buyers step in at the most recent minor demand and price makes a new higher low.

- When price is rising, but with dips which spike down, you are seeing compression in the up move. When you see this, you know that the buys orders are being consumed on the pull-backs in the up move.

- When price is falling but with spikes up, you are seeing compression in the down move. When you see this, you know that the sell orders are being consumed on the rallies in the down move.
